extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, novelists, playwrights and fiction writers studying story structure and craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for designing story structure across beats, scenes, sequences, acts, and the overall story (Archplot/Miniplot/Antiplot) primarily for screenwriters but applicable to fiction writers. Focuses on how events must change value-charged conditions through conflict and how formal choices shape audience experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story Event
rubrics_metrics.description: A Story Event creates meaningful change in the life situation of a character that is expressed and experienced in terms of a value and ACHIEVED THROUGH CONFLICT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and explanation: coincidence has a place but a story cannot be built of accidental events alone; The Rainmaker is an example where inner, social and environmental conflicts culminate in a meaningful change (coaxing rain). Emphasizes that change must be value-charged and motivated through conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene
rubrics_metrics.description: A SCENE is an action through conflict in more or less continuous time and space that turns the value-charged condition of a character's life on at least one value with a degree of perceptible significance. Ideally, every scene is a STORY EVENT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How to evaluate/shape scenes: ask what value is at stake at the opening (love? truth? etc.) and how it is charged (positive/negative/both); note the value at the close and compare. If the value-charged condition is unchanged, the scene is a nonevent and likely exposition — a disciplined writer should trash it or weave information elsewhere. Principle: "No scene that doesn't turn." Examples: the "lovers break up" scene (turns from positive to negative); camera setups that intensify but do not change values are not true scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical number of Story Events (scenes)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a typical film, the writer will choose forty to sixty Story Events; a novelist may want more than sixty; a playwright rarely as many as forty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these counts as a planning guideline when structuring a screenplay versus a novel or play; choose numbers appropriate to medium and storytelling goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat
rubrics_metrics.description: A BEAT is an exchange of behavior in action/reaction. Beat by Beat these changing behaviors shape the turning of a scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beats are the smallest element of structure. Scenes are built from distinct beats (different behaviors/action–reaction). Example: the "lovers break up" scene is built around six beats (teasing → insults → threats/daring → pleading/ridiculing → violence → Turning Point). Beats should lead to the scene's Turning Point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: A SEQUENCE is a series of scenes—generally two to five—that culminates with greater impact than any previous scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequences deliver a more powerful, determinant change than individual scenes. Title each sequence to clarify its purpose (e.g., "getting the job"). Use sequences to dramatize character and context beyond a single scene; the capping scene of a sequence delivers a Sequence Climax with greater impact. Example: three-scene sequence taking a woman from NO JOB to JOB, each scene turning on its own value but subordinated to THE JOB as the sequence's overriding value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act
rubrics_metrics.description: An ACT is a series of sequences that peaks in a climactic scene which causes a major reversal of values, more powerful in its impact than any previous sequence or scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish degrees of change: scenes cause minor/significant change; sequence climaxes cause moderate/greater change; act climaxes cause major reversals affecting inner life, relationships, fortunes, or combinations thereof. Use act structure to stage rising impact toward the story climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story
rubrics_metrics.description: A Story is a series of acts. When you compare the value-charged condition in a character's life at the beginning of the story to that at the end, you should see the arc of the film — the great sweep of change from one condition to a changed condition at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final condition must be absolute and irreversible. Scene→sequence→act→story hierarchy: let the smallest elements do their job to serve the deep purpose of the telling; build minor, moderate, and major changes cumulatively to the Story Climax. Examples illustrate arcs from optimistic protagonist to a changed, more corrupt or transformed end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story Climax (Closed Ending)
rubrics_metrics.description: STORY CLIMAX: a story is a series of acts that build to a last act climax or story climax which brings about absolute and irreversible change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Story Climax that answers all questions raised and satisfies audience emotion is a CLOSED ENDING. The climax of the last act must create irreversible change; earlier changes (scene, sequence, act) conceivably could be reversed, but not the final climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make every phrase do its job
rubrics_metrics.description: Let every phrase of dialogue or line of description either turn behavior and action or set up the conditions for change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Micro-level discipline: every line should either advance a turn or set conditions for future change. If the smallest elements are efficient, the deep purpose of the telling will be served; otherwise cut or repurpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot (definition and responsibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: To PLOT means to navigate through the dangerous terrain of story and when confronted by a dozen branching possibilities to choose the correct path. Plot is the writer's choice of events and their design in time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plotting involves selecting, excluding, and ordering events; good plotting is not mere twistsmanship but careful selection and patterning through time. Examples: TENDER MERCIES is exquisitely plotted; missing or superfluous scenes can collapse the intended inner journey. Plot implies causal design rather than random accumulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical Design / Archplot
rubrics_metrics.description: CLASSICAL DESIGN means a story built around an active protagonist who struggles against primarily external forces of antagonism to pursue his or her desire through continuous time within a consistent and causally connected fictional reality to a closed ending of absolute, irreversible change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This collection of principles is called the Archplot. Archplot characteristics listed include: Causality, Closed Ending, Linear Time, External Conflict, Single Protagonist, Consistent Reality, Active Protagonist. Archplot is the dominant, international form of cinema and satisfies audiences with a rounded experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miniplot / Minimalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Miniplot (Minimalism) begins with elements of Classical Design but reduces them—shrinking or compressing, trimming or truncating prominent features of the Archplot; it strives for simplicity and economy while retaining enough classical elements to satisfy the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Miniplot often leaves endings somewhat open, emphasizes interior values and inner conflict, and may use nonlinear or compressed time; it must still be beautifully executed. Examples include TENDER MERCIES, PARIS, TEXAS; narrative documentaries can also be Miniplot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antiplot / Anti-structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Antiplot reverses the Classical, contradicting traditional forms to exploit or ridicule formal principles; antiplot-makers tend toward extravagance and self-conscious overstatement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antiplot substitutes coincidence, fragmentation, and open forms; it often scrambles time, disconnects characters from external causality, and creates open or unresolved endings. Examples include UN CHIEN ANDALOU, PERSONA, LAST YEAR AT MARIENBAD, and other avant-garde/European films.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed Ending (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Story Climax of absolute, irreversible change that answers all questions raised by the telling and satisfies all audience emotion is a CLOSED ENDING.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a closed ending all questions are answered and the audience leaves with a rounded, closed experience. Use closed endings when you intend to resolve all dramatic queries and emotional arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open Ending (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Story Climax that leaves a question or two unanswered and some emotion unfulfilled is an OPEN ENDING.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open endings may leave a small number of answerable questions or emotional residue for the audience to satisfy. Open doesn't mean unfinished chaos; the unanswered elements must be plausibly resolvable by the audience's imagination. Example: PARIS, TEXAS closes some arcs but leaves others open intentionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: External vs Internal Conflict (focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Archplot emphasizes external conflict (struggles with people, social institutions, or the physical world); Miniplot emphasizes internal conflict (battles within thoughts and feelings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose emphasis according to desired design: action-oriented stories foreground public values (freedom/slavery, justice/injustice); education/inner-arc stories foreground interior values (self-awareness/self-deception). Examples: THE ROAD WARRIOR (external) vs THE ACCIDENTAL TOURIST (internal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single vs Multiple Protagonists
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical design usually places a single protagonist at the heart of the telling; splitting the film into many smaller stories creates a Multiplot/Miniplot variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single-protagonist stories concentrate screentime and roller-coaster dynamics; multiplot softens the telling by distributing attention across several protagonists (e.g., PARENTHOOD, SHORT CUTS). Choose structure that fits thematic and emotional aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active vs Passive Protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: An ACTIVE PROTAGONIST, in pursuit of desire, takes action in direct conflict with people and the world around him. A PASSIVE PROTAGONIST is outwardly inactive while pursuing desire inwardly, in conflict with aspects of his or her own nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active protagonists drive external plot; passive protagonists require interior emphasis or surrounding dramatic events to sustain interest. Example: PELLE THE CONQUEROR uses a passive child viewpoint to observe tragic events offscreen, softening melodrama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear vs Nonlinear Time
rubrics_metrics.description: A story told with events arranged into a temporal order the audience can follow is told in LINEAR TIME. A story that scrambles or blurs temporal continuity so the audience cannot sort before/after is told in NONLINEAR TIME.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archplot prefers linear time (flashbacks used so audience can place events); antiplot often fragments time (flash-forwards/flashbacks mixed) to disconnect characters from the world. Example: BAD TIMING's scrambled temporal structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causality vs Coincidence
rubrics_metrics.description: CAUSALITY drives a story in which motivated actions cause effects that in turn become causes of further effects, interlinking conflicts in a chain reaction toward the Story Climax. COINCIDENCE drives a fictional world where unmotivated actions trigger events that do not cause further effects, fragmenting the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer causality for coherent Archplot design and meaningful interconnectedness; antiplot often employs coincidence to express disconnectedness and absurdity (example: AFTER HOURS). Use causality to create meaningful cause-effect chains; avoid unmotivated coincidences as primary plot drivers unless intentionally aiming for antistructure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent vs Inconsistent Realities
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistent Versus Inconsistent Realities (heading / dimension of formal difference).
